tldr: To achieve both smooth movement and fast online error correction under delayed sensory feedback, the authors proposed a control model that multiplexes position, velocity, and error signals and feeds them back to the cerebral cortex via the cerebellum. The model reproduced behavior and neural activity matching monkey experimental data.
hero_caption: Schematic of the proposed cortico-cerebellar loop architecture. The cerebellar model (mossy-fibre dimensional expansion and parallel-fibre–Purkinje cell synapses) receives commands from a cortical RNN and delayed sensory feedback. It sends delay-compensated predictive and error signals back to the cortex, achieving stable online control and learning.
overview:
Sensory delay—the time it takes for sensory information to arrive—is a major headache in both robotics and biological systems. Using delayed signals directly in feedback control causes overshooting and oscillations, leading to unstable movements. Classical cerebellar models explained that delay could be compensated by a forward model predicting future sensory outcomes from motor commands. However, that alone could not properly explain the rapid online trajectory corrections during movement or the fast trial-by-trial adaptation observed in biological organisms.

To address this, the authors turned to recent neuroscience findings. First, the cerebellum multiplexes multiple streams of information—such as position, velocity, and error—rather than encoding just a single physical quantity. Second, delayed sensory errors do not enter the cerebral cortex directly; they return to the cortex via the cerebellar loop. In this work, the authors built a closed-loop control model combining a recurrent neural network (RNN) representing the motor cortex with a feedforward network modeling cerebellar neural circuitry.

When tested on a visuomotor rotation task mimicking monkey reaching experiments, models predicting single variables (position only or velocity only) failed to re-aim toward the target mid-movement. In contrast, using a multiplexed representation of position, velocity, and error reproduced smooth, rapid trajectory corrections just like those of monkeys. Furthermore, routing sensory feedback through the cerebellum rather than directly into the cortex greatly stabilized learning and neatly accounted for the biphasic neural activity patterns observed in the motor cortex.
contributions: Demonstrated that multiplexing position, velocity, and position error from the cerebellum back to the cortex enables fast online trajectory corrections even under substantial sensory delays.

Reproduced motor adaptation across two distinct timescales—rapid trial-by-trial error reduction and slow feedforward updates—by routing delayed sensory feedback through the cerebellar loop rather than directly to the cerebral cortex.
Naturally captured the biphasic population dynamics observed in primary motor cortex (M1), featuring an early feedforward-driven peak and a late feedback-driven peak, via cerebellar feedback.

Computationally demonstrated an error-dependent gating mechanism where feedback activity transiently surges only in early adaptation when errors are large, and automatically decays as learning progresses.

sections.heading: Why Can Biological Systems Move Quickly and Adapt Despite Delays?
sections.summary: Transmission delays in sensory signals severely destabilize feedback control. Focusing on cortical-cerebellar cooperation, this section introduces the core question: how multiplexed representations and cerebellar feedback pathways reconcile delay compensation with fast adaptation.
sections.details:
Robust feedback control is essential for robots and biological organisms to move nimbly in dynamic environments. However, real-world systems inevitably suffer from sensory delays. Corrections based on out-of-date information arrive at the wrong time, causing overcorrection and control instability.

Biological motor systems face sensory delays of several tens to over a hundred milliseconds. Yet they perform rapid online error corrections during movement and rapid motor adaptation across trials with remarkable ease. Classical neuroscience posited that the cerebral cortex generates motor commands while the cerebellum acts as a forward model, predicting sensory outcomes from motor commands to cancel out delays.

However, classical models could not fully explain the millisecond-scale online corrections or trial-by-trial adaptation dynamics seen in biological systems. Recent experiments have revealed that cerebellar output has a multiplexed structure carrying both kinematic information (position and velocity) and task error simultaneously, while motor cortical neural populations display characteristic activity shifts during adaptation. This study provides a clear answer to the fundamental question of how delayed sensory feedback should be routed and represented within the cortico-cerebellar circuit, using a biologically plausible RNN model.

sections.heading: At the Crossroads of Classical Cerebellar Models and Deep Learning
sections.summary: This section reviews classical cerebellar theory from Marr–Albus–Ito to recent RNN-based motor cortex modeling, highlighting the importance of sensory delay routing paths often overlooked in prior RNN studies.
sections.details:
Research into the computational functions of the cerebellum originated with the Marr–Albus–Ito framework and has long explored the acquisition of forward models and error-driven learning mechanisms. Behavioral experiments have also shown that motor adaptation spans multiple distinct timescales: fast online error correction and slow internal model updating.

In recent years, continuous-time RNNs have become popular for modeling cortical dynamics, successfully reproducing muscle activity and endpoint movements. However, most of these earlier studies fed sensory feedback directly into cortical RNN units, bypassing the cerebellum.

While some prior studies incorporated cerebellar modules, the exact wiring and functional role of delayed sensory signals remained unclear. This paper directly compares feeding sensory feedback directly into the cortex versus processing it through the cerebellum, positioning cerebellar signal transformation as the key to achieving both biological plausibility and control stability.

sections.heading: Closed-Loop Design Combining a Cortical RNN and a Cerebellar Module
sections.summary: This section details the 2D reaching task modeled after monkey experiments, the network architecture comprising the cerebral cortex (RNN) and cerebellum (sparse expansion + linear readout), and the learning procedure combining local learning rules.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Task Setup
The authors designed an environment simulating a delayed-reach center-out task commonly used in monkey experiments. Start and target positions were randomly sampled from a uniform distribution over $[-6, 6]$. The target velocity profile followed a smooth, bell-shaped sigmoid function (time constant $\kappa = 10\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$). A single trial lasted 300 steps (about 3 seconds), with a random hold period of 1.2 to 1.7 seconds inserted in between. To evaluate motor adaptation, a visuomotor rotation (VR) perturbation was introduced, rotating the endpoint movement direction by 30 degrees.

### 3.2 Network Architecture
The motor cortex was modeled as a continuous-time RNN with $N = 50$ units, a time constant $\tau = 50\,\mathrm{ms}$, and a step size $dt = 10\,\mathrm{ms}$. The cortical state equation is given by:
$$\tau \dot{h}(t) = -h(t) + W_h \Phi(h(t)) + W_{in} x(t) + W_{fb} c(t)$$
Hand velocity $y(t)$ was read out linearly from cortical states, and position $p(t)$ was obtained by integrating velocity over time. The cerebellar module received the delayed cortical state $h(t-\Delta)$ and delayed sensory feedback $s(t-\Delta) = p^*(t-\Delta) - p(t-\Delta)$. The delay was fixed at $\Delta = 120\,\mathrm{ms}$ to match physiological delays in biological systems. Mossy-fibre weights $W_{MF}$ expanded inputs into a high-dimensional sparse space at a 1:20 ratio, and parallel-fibre weights $W_{PF}$ sent corrective predictive signals $c(t)$ back to the cortex.

### 3.3 Adaptation and Learning Rules
Instead of backpropagation, the cortical weights were updated using a biologically plausible local eligibility trace rule. Weights were updated at the end of each trial by combining accumulated past neural activity with the cerebellar feedback signal. Meanwhile, parallel-fibre weights $W_{PF}$ in the cerebellum were trained via gradient descent with the Adam optimizer, guided by the error between delayed targets and internal predictions (mimicking climbing-fibre input).

### 3.4 Two-Stage Training Procedure
Training proceeded in two stages. During the first 100 epochs (pre-training phase), the cortical feedback weights $W_{fb}$ were held fixed so that the cerebellum could acquire a stable predictive representation without disrupting cortical dynamics. Over the subsequent 500 epochs, cortical and cerebellar learning ran simultaneously, establishing closed-loop cortico-cerebellar adaptation.

sections.heading: Dramatic Effects of Multiplexed Representations and Cerebellar Feedback
sections.summary: Single predictive signals failed to correct reaches under a 120 ms delay. However, multiplexing position, velocity, and error reproduced monkey trajectory corrections. Furthermore, cerebellar feedback achieved both rapid error reduction and biphasic cortical activity.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Multiplexed Representations Enable Online Trajectory Corrections
First, the authors compared the content of the predictive signals sent from the cerebellum to the cortex. Single-variable models predicting only velocity, only position, or only position error generated smooth trajectories, but they drifted parallel to the target under the 30-degree visual perturbation, failing to re-aim mid-movement (Figure F2 B).

In contrast, only the multiplexed model combining position, velocity, and position error successfully curved sharply mid-reach toward the target after perturbation, mirroring monkey behavioral data (Figure F2 C). Position provided the current state, velocity provided future predictions for delay compensation, and position error provided the driving force back toward the target, establishing a robust control loop. When cerebellar prediction was omitted and delayed error was fed back directly, severe overcorrection and trajectory oscillations occurred (Figure F2 D).

### 4.2 Separation of Adaptation Timescales Across Trials
Motor adaptation exhibits dual timescales: rapid elimination of endpoint error and slow updating of the initial take-off angle. The model providing sensory feedback to the cerebellum showed a gradual decrease in take-off error that matched experimental data closely (Figure F3 B).

In a comparison model where sensory input to the cerebellum was cut off, excessive optimization pressure fell solely on cortical feedforward commands, causing an unnaturally steep change in take-off angle. Because the cerebellum receives delayed errors and corrects movements mid-flight, the initial launch command does not need to change abruptly, producing biological dual-rate adaptation.

### 4.3 Cerebellar Routing Reproduces Cortical Biphasic Dynamics
Population activity in the primary motor cortex (M1) is known to be biphasic, with an early feedforward peak immediately after movement onset and a delayed feedback-driven corrective peak. The proposed model routing sensory feedback through the cerebellum produced a clear late peak in cortical RNN activity, matching experimental data (Figure F4 B). Direct sensory input to the cortex also generated a late peak, but it led to major differences in learning stability, as described next.

### 4.4 Error-Dependent Gating and Learning Stability
When sensory input entered the cortex directly, strong feedback activity persisted constantly during baseline periods and after adaptation. With the cerebellar-routed model, however, feedback activity surged transiently only during early adaptation when errors were large (right after perturbation), and automatically decayed to baseline levels as adaptation progressed (Figure F5 A).

This autonomous, error-dependent suppression reduced variance in the learning curve, allowing smooth and rapid convergence to zero error (Figure F5 B). Rather than disrupting core cortical dynamics with raw delayed sensory signals, appropriately processing and gating them through the cerebellum proved decisively advantageous.

captions.F2: Comparison of monkey reaching trajectories (A) with various models. Single-variable predictions (velocity/position/error) (B) drift parallel to the target without correcting, while delayed feedback without the cerebellum (D) oscillates. Only the multiplexed model combining position, velocity, and position error (C) faithfully reproduces the monkey's behavior of making a sharp mid-movement turn toward the target during early adaptation.
captions.F3: Comparison of trial-by-trial adaptation dynamics. (B) In take-off error evolution, the model with cerebellar feedback (orange) decreases gradually, matching experimental data (black), whereas the model without feedback (blue) adapts unnaturally fast. (C) Endpoint error is kept substantially lower from early adaptation onward thanks to cerebellar feedback.
captions.F4: Time-course comparison of population activity changes in the motor cortex RNN. In addition to the initial rise after the Go cue, the model receiving sensory feedback via the cerebellum (orange) forms a distinct second peak (feedback peak) around 0.75 seconds, matching monkey M1 data (black).
captions.F5: Feedback activity across adaptation (A) and inter-trial error convergence (B). The direct cortical input model (green) maintains constant feedback activity and shows unstable learning. In contrast, the cerebellar-routed model (orange) exhibits error-dependent gating where activity rises only right after perturbation, enabling the smoothest and fastest convergence of error to zero.

sections.heading: Bio-Inspired Delay Compensation Guidelines for Robotics and AI
sections.summary: This section summarizes the findings and outlines their potential beyond understanding biological motor learning, pointing toward modular control architectures for robots and reinforcement learning agents facing sensory delays.
sections.details:
This study computationally demonstrates that multiplexed sensory feedback representations mediated by the cerebellum are essential for motor control and adaptation under sensory delays.

Feeding raw, delayed sensory signals directly into a primary controller (cerebral cortex) causes overcorrection and destabilizes learning. However, when a cerebellar module integrates position, velocity, and error to compensate for delays ahead of time, and gates error signals so they flow only when and as strongly as needed, fast online correction and long-term adaptation coexist with remarkable elegance.

This design philosophy offers powerful insights not only for neuroscience, but also for real-world robotics and deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents. In physical environments with communication latency and sensor processing delays, dividing labor by running a specialized cerebellar-type module for delay compensation and error prediction in parallel with the primary controller (feedforward policy)—without disrupting its core dynamics—provides an excellent blueprint for building delay-resilient, dependable control systems.

takeaways: In delayed environments, feedback control based on a single predictive quantity is insufficient; a multiplexed representation combining position (state), velocity (delay compensation), and error (driving force) is essential.

Routing delayed sensory error signals through the cerebellar loop (compensator) rather than feeding them directly into the cerebral cortex (primary controller) dramatically stabilizes learning dynamics and accelerates convergence.
Interposing a cerebellar module autonomously achieves error-dependent gating, where feedback intervenes only early on when errors are large and naturally withdraws once learning is complete.
limitations: Evaluations were limited to a relatively simple 2D planar center-out reaching task; verification on real-world, high-DOF articulated robots involving complex joint torques, contacts, and disturbances has not yet been conducted.

Parallel-fibre weights in the cerebellar module were trained using standard Adam gradient descent, representing a biological simplification compared to the local learning rule used in the cortical RNN.
Feedback delay was treated as a fixed 120 ms value; robustness against network jitter and variable delays typical of real communication environments was not verified.
